{"id": "bc685eb9-5028-4621-b42f-2e19ca09c1a7", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_LFLDCxlWkuXhx7brXnHQaO", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"Find the changes that could explain the symptoms, or confirm whether and when a specific change happened.\\\\n\\\\n## CloudTrail: `lookup_cloudtrail_events`\\\\n\\\\nCloudTrail calls through `use_aws` are blocked; `lookup_cloudtrail_events` is the route. It returns management events from the last 90 days, newest first, for one account and region per call.\\\\n\\\\n- Each call returns at most about 10,000 characters of events. Every event carries its full CloudTrailEvent JSON, so a call often holds only a handful of events. When it stops early it returns `continuation_timestamp`; pass that as the next `end_time` to page to older events.\\\\n- With no attribute, the tool returns only write events (`ReadOnly` is `false`), which is what a change timeline needs. LookupEvents takes one attribute per call, so passing `attribute_key` and `attribute_value` (EventSource, ResourceName, Username, EventName and so on) replaces that default, and read-only calls then share the size cap with the writes. Use an attribute to follow one resource, user or event name.\\\\n- Narrow before you page: exclude noisy event names and use windows of about 15 minutes. Excluded events do not count toward the size cap. `jmespath_filter` runs after the cap, so it shrinks the output but does not return more events.\\\\n- Passing `exclude_event_names` replaces the default exclusions (`CreateLogStream`, `Invoke`, `InvokeExecution`, `UpdateInstanceInformation`, `PutObject`); include them again if you still want them dropped.\\\\n- LookupEvents allows 2 requests per second per account and region, and one tool call may page several times, so run at most 2 CloudTrail calls at once.\\\\n- Start near the symptom onset and work backward until you find changes that address the question or have covered the requested timeframe.\\\\n\\\\nKubernetes events come from `use_kubectl`.
